name: Prader-Willi Syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Holm et al. Consensus Diagnostic Criteria (1993) with Genetic Confirmation

criteria.description: Feeding problems in infancy requiring special feeding techniques
Excessive weight gain between 1-6 years with central obesity
Characteristic facial features (narrow bifrontal diameter, almond-shaped eyes, thin upper lip, down-turned mouth)
Developmental delay / mild to moderate intellectual disability (IQ 60-70 typical)
Hyperphagia (excessive appetite) and food-seeking behavior after age 2-4 years
Genetic confirmation: loss of paternal expression of 15q11-q13 region

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical suspicion confirmed by DNA methylation analysis showing absence of paternally expressed 15q11-q13. Methylation testing detects >99% of cases.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Three genetic mechanisms: paternal deletion (~70%), maternal uniparental disomy (~25%), imprinting center defect (~2-5%). Clinical criteria are scored (major = 1 point, minor = 0.5 point); >= 5 points in children >3 years or >= 8 points in adults triggers testing.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Neonatal hypotonia transitioning to childhood hyperphagia and obesity
pathognomonic.notes: The biphasic nutritional phenotype is highly characteristic: failure to thrive in infancy followed by insatiable appetite

common.notes: Typically begins between ages 2-6 years; insatiable appetite is central feature
Growth hormone deficiency in most patients

occasional.symptomName: Behavioral problems (temper tantrums, stubbornness, OCD-like features)
Sleep disturbances (central and obstructive sleep apnea, excessive daytime sleepiness)

rare.notes: Can be fatal; reduced pain sensitivity delays recognition

laboratory: Low growth hormone levels and/or IGF-1
Elevated ghrelin levels (paradoxically elevated despite obesity)
Elevated HbA1c / glucose if diabetes develops
imaging: DEXA scan showing reduced bone mineral density
Brain MRI may show pituitary hypoplasia
genetic: DNA methylation analysis at 15q11-q13 (detects >99% of cases; first-line test)
Paternal deletion (~70%) detected by FISH, MLPA, or chromosomal microarray

distinguishingFeatures: Severe intellectual disability with absent speech

redFlags: Acute gastric dilation from binge eating (can be fatal; high pain threshold delays recognition)
Severe obesity-related complications (type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea, cor pulmonale)
Unexplained sudden death (possibly related to adrenal insufficiency or respiratory failure)
Water intoxication from excessive fluid intake
references: Cassidy SB, et al. Prader-Willi syndrome. Genet Med. 2012;14(1):10-26.
Goldstone AP, et al. Recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Prader-Willi syndrome. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2008;93(11):4183-4197.
Butler MG, et al. Prader-Willi syndrome - clinical genetics, diagnosis and treatment approaches: an update. Curr Pediatr Rev. 2019;15(4):207-244.
Driscoll DJ, et al. Prader-Willi Syndrome. GeneReviews. Updated 2017.
